common_name: Pipestone Plum (University of Minnesota Cold-Hardy Hybrid Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pipestone is not self-fertile and needs a compatible Japanese-American hybrid plum blooming at the same time, such as Superior or Toka, for reliable cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible Japanese-American hybrid pollinizer such as Superior or Toka nearby, since Pipestone is not reliably self-fruitful. Pipestone was released by the University of Minnesota fruit breeding program from a cross of Burbank with a Prunus salicina x Wolf seedling, part of the same long-running Minnesota plum-breeding effort that combined Japanese plum quality with the extreme cold hardiness of native American plum to fill a gap for northern gardeners where standard Japanese and European plums winter-kill. Pipestone bears very large, red-skinned, clingstone fruit with sweet, juicy yellow flesh under a notably thick, tough skin that holds firm until it splits open in a burst of juice at full ripeness. The tree is exceptionally productive and among the hardiest named plums available, making it a dependable choice for the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains where many stone fruits fail. Thin heavy fruit sets to improve size and reduce limb breakage, and prune in late winter to an open form for good light and air circulation.
sources: University of Minnesota Fruit Research Extension

common_name: Paul's Scarlet Hawthorn (Crimson Cloud, Double Red English Hawthorn)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Paul's Scarlet is grown for its fully double, rose-red May flowers rather than for fruit, since the doubled flowers set little to no haws.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Paul's Scarlet, also sold in North America as Crimson Cloud, arose as a sport of the older double-pink midland hawthorn Rosea Flore Pleno found in an English garden in the 1850s, and it quickly became one of the most popular flowering hawthorns in cultivation, later earning the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. In mid-to-late spring the thorny branches are smothered in fully double, deep rose-red to scarlet flowers carried in dense clusters, a far showier and more saturated display than the simple white or pale pink blooms of the wild species, followed in autumn by dark green foliage that turns red. Because the flowers are double and largely sterile, the tree sets few if any of the small red haws typical of single-flowered hawthorns, so its garden value rests almost entirely on the spectacular spring bloom and on its dense, twiggy, thorny branching, which still offers good nesting cover for birds. It tolerates a wide range of soils from acidic to alkaline and adapts to both moist and fairly dry sites once established. As a grafted named clone it must be propagated vegetatively, since seedlings revert to single flowers.

planting.note: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting and move to the garden after frost danger passes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Rainbow is a bisexual F1 hybrid derived from a cross of the transgenic 'SunUp' papaya with the traditional Hawaiian cultivar 'Kapoho,' bred specifically for resistance to papaya ringspot virus.

directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting or sow directly in warm soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Rainbow is the transgenic, papaya ringspot virus-resistant papaya developed in Hawaii after the virus devastated nearly all of the state's main papaya-growing region in the early 1990s. Researchers engineered papaya lines carrying a gene for the virus's own coat protein, which triggers a resistance response in the plant; the resulting transgenic line became the parent cultivar SunUp. Rainbow itself is a bisexual F1 hybrid produced by crossing SunUp with the traditional, non-transgenic Kapoho cultivar, combining reliable ringspot virus resistance with Kapoho's familiar yellow-orange, sweet, small-seed-cavity fruit quality. Rainbow and SunUp were released to Hawaiian growers in 1998 and are widely credited with saving Hawaii's papaya industry from collapse within a few years of release. The compact tree begins bearing within roughly seven to ten months of germination in warm conditions, and fruit should be picked as the skin begins to turn from green to yellow, then allowed to finish ripening at room temperature. As with other papayas, protect from frost and provide consistent moisture and a balanced fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

common_name: Silver Ripple Peperomia (Silvery Ripple-Leaf Radiator Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light in well-drained, peat-based potting mix; Silver Ripple carries deeply corrugated, shimmering silvery-green leaves with a hint of red blush on the newest growth, a cooler, more metallic cultivar within the caperata group alongside 'Rosso' and 'Luna Red'.

directions: Grow in bright to moderate indirect light in a well-drained, peat-based potting mix, allowing the soil to dry slightly between waterings, since this semi-succulent cultivar of Peperomia caperata is more forgiving of missed waterings than of soggy soil. Silver Ripple bears the same deeply corrugated, heart-shaped leaves typical of ripple peperomias, but in a shimmering silvery-green tone with a delicate flush of red on the newest, smallest leaves, giving it a cooler, more metallic presence than the plain green-and-silver species or the darker-colored Rosso and Luna Red cultivars already common in the trade. The compact, bushy rosette typically stays under ten inches tall and wide, making it well suited to small pots, dish gardens, and crowded windowsills. Like other caperata cultivars it occasionally sends up slender, greenish-white, rat-tail-like flower spikes, grown incidentally rather than for display, since the corrugated foliage is the main ornamental feature. Keep it out of direct sun, which scorches the thin leaf surface, and propagate by dividing congested rosettes or rooting leaf cuttings in a barely moist mix.
